The College of Nursing offers 3 nurse practitioner (NP) specialty tracks within its MS program and its Post-MS Certificate Program. These include Adult-Gerontology Primary Care NP, Family NP and Psychiatric-Mental Health NP (PMHNP). The first two of these specialties focus on primary care and are identical in terms of total credits in the MS Program (42) and very similar in terms of coursework and other program requirements. The PMHNP specialty track is the newest specialty track offered within the MS program

2 and currently requires 48 - 49 credits.
Having just graduated their first few graduates in the PMHNP specialty track, the PMHNP program faculty, the MS/DNP Program Committee and Associate Dean Kathy Hutchinson all agreed that revisions were needed within the PMHNP specialty track to address 3 issues.
The 3 issues and proposed changes to the PMHNP specialty track are outlined below and shown in Appendix A: (1) the credit allocations for some of the courses within the PMHNP specialty (e.g., NUR 545) needed to be corrected to be more consistent with university standards and other course offerings within the program.
NUR 545 focuses on psychiatric-mental health care for children, adolescents and families and is a 2 credit course.
In contrast, NUR 513 focuses on psychiatric-mental health care for adults and is a 3 credit course.

The didactic NP specialty courses in the other NP specialty tracks are all 3 credit courses. (2) In addition to correcting the inconsistency in credit allocations to didactic courses, the faculty and MS/DNP cmte. sought to address uneven distribution of clinical practicum credits across the PMHNP clinical courses (NUR 514, 546 and 547) and align these credits with those in the other NP specialty tracks.
The current PMHNP specialty requires 500- 600+ clinical hours and the 3 clinical courses total 15 credits.
In comparison, the other specialty tracks require similar clinical hours but allocate only 12 credits across their 3 clinical courses. (3) In order to be consistent with recommendations from our accrediting body (The American Association of Colleges of Nursing / CCNE), the CON implemented a single course addressing Advanced Health Assessment / Physical Assessment Across the Lifespan (NUR 530) In Fall, 2021.
This 4 credit didactic and lab course will now be completed by students in all 3 nurse practitioner specialty tracks in the MS program.
In the past, PMHNP students took an abbreviated 3 credit course in health assessment (NUR 501).

This change alone would result in an additional 1 credit increase to the PMHNP track of the MS curriculum.
The number of credits for this specialty track is already high.
Addressing the issues in (1) and (3) above would result in a 1 - 2 credit increase in the number of credits in the PMHNP specialty track.
Balancing this against the need to reduce clinical credits in (2) above, would result in an overall reduction in the number of credits for the PMHNP specialty track in the MS program from 48-49 to 47.
The individual course syllabi have been revised to reflect changes in pre-requisites (NUR 530 replaces NUR 501 as a pre-requisite for all the specialty courses [e.g., NUR 513, 514, 545, 546 and 547]).
The course descriptions have been clarified and the course objectives reviewed and edited slightly.
The descriptions for the clinical practicum courses (NUR 514, 546, 547) have been abbreviated and written more broadly to indicate that these courses focus on the application of previous and concurrent learning in a variety of practice settings.

Retention and Graduation Requirements Starting with the first professional year (P1), the College of Pharmacy calculates its own grade point average (GPA), an average which differs from the GPA calculated by the University.
The grade point average calculated by the College includes only required didactic pharmacy courses and is called the quality point average (QPA).
Good academic standing requires a QPA of 2.3 or higher, a semester QPA of 2.30 or higher, and a grade of at least C- in each required pharmacy course.
A student will automatically be placed on probation when they do not meet one or more of the good standing requirements.
Furthermore, a student whose cumulative QPA falls below a 2.20 at the end of any semester will be dismissed from the program.
A student on probation for two consecutive semesters without returning to good standing also will be dismissed from the program.

A student who receives a grade below C- in any required pharmacy course or whose QPA falls between 2.20 and 2.30 at the end of a semester will be reviewed by the Scholastic Standing Committee and presented with a remediation plan that must be successfully completed in order to progress in the curriculum.
Remediation plans will be designed to meet program standards (QPA and minimum grade requirements) and may include repeating courses, additional self study and or faculty assessment of proficiency through assignments and examinations.
Remediation plans will be developed by the Scholastic Standing Committee taking into account the student’s QPA, length of time enrolled in the program(i.e., P1, P2, or P3 status), the number and types of deficiencies, and trends in academic performance.
A student who is not successful in completing the remediation plan developed by the Scholastic Standing Committee will be dismissed from the

Criminal Background Checks.
All students must undergo a criminal background check annually during the professional (P1 to P4) years of the program using the College’s approved vendor.
The criminal background check must be completed prior to the fall semester of each professional year and before any Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experience (IPPE) is initiated.
Many hospitals, clinical facilities, and other professional sites that participate in both the IPPE and advanced pharmacy practice experience (APPE) programs require certification that students have a clear criminal record (or a criminal record which, due to the timing or nature of the criminal behavior, or the relevant circumstances, does not, in the judgment of the site preclude the student’s participation in the practicum experience at their site) prior to initiating pharmacy practice experiences.

Students with criminal records, therefore, should be aware that their criminal record may preclude their participation in clinical experiences at some sites, and as a result, their progression to meet the degree requirements may be impeded.
Drug Testing.
Many hospitals, clinical facilities, and other professional sites that participate in both the introductory practice experiences (IPPE) and advanced practice experiences (APPE) require students to undergo a drug test.
Students who test positive for an illegal drug will be denied positions at these sites.
As a result, their progression to meet the degree requirements will be impeded.
Intern License Requirement.
Registration as an intern pharmacist is a requirement of the program; therefore all students in the professional Pharm.D. program must hold a valid Rhode Island intern license when they enter the fall semester of their first professional year and before any Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experience (IPPE) is initiated.
The Rhode Island intern license must be maintained throughout the professional program (P1 to P4 years).

Students completing IPPE or APPE experiences in other states must obtain an intern license through the board of pharmacy of the state(s) in which they have those practice experiences.
Intern licensure in Massachusetts is recommended for all students, but not required.
To be eligible for an intern license, students must be currently enrolled in a pharmacy program.
Intern licenses must be returned to the board if a student withdraws or takes a leave of absence from the college.
Applications for an intern license also normally require the applicant to disclose, and provide an explanation of, any criminal conviction (or any plea or other form of admission or acceptance of responsibility for criminal conduct, including driving under the influence), as well as any state disciplinary action involving or affecting the applicant’s license to practice, any other pending state charges or investigations relating to the applicant, and any adverse proceeding or action relating to the applicant’s membership in a professional society.
